Lovecraftian to the fishbone, Dredge regresses the high seas to catch a glimpse of the abysmal terror in a delightfully casual fishing adventure.

[h3][i]***[/i][/h3]

Dredge possesses a strange quality of being sweet and almost too casual while giving justice to one of the world's most renowned horror writers, HP Minecraft. Or is it Lovecraft? :-) Anyway, the best part about the game is that it does not pressure or punish the player [i]too much[/i]; it gives time to explore and unwind and still manages to convey what makes Lovecraftian horror unique through a simple day and night cycle. Sanity is fragile. Every night, sinister sea fog becomes a conductor and a metaphor for a fogged mind. Is there salvation when you fight the abyss of madness in and around you? Not gonna lie: sometimes I think we already live in a Lovecraftian world…Take these themes away from the game, and you will end up with an arcade fishing simulator.

Core mechanics revolve. If you think that statement is missing something, I can assure you it is not. Several mini-games depict "fishing" or "dredging," and all constitute a wheel with revolving indicators. Not one is even remotely difficult. The main idea is to give a sense of time passing by and revert your focus from the clock rather than give a formidable challenge. The tricky part is to get the necessary equipment and have it on board if you require some particular catch and, well, locating the fishing spot in the first place. Some fish are nocturnal, forcing the fisherman to step out of his comfort zone. That is when things become obscure. Naturally, the fisherman should confront his demons: in the deep of the night, the deep of the ocean, and the deep of the mind.

Dredge is the only game where I willingly sail into a cosmic horror abyss just because I really need to upgrade my little fishing boat. It is a delightful mix of 'calming coastal simulator' and 'please stop staring at me with too many eyes,' leaving me equal parts terrified and oddly satisfied with my catch.

[h2]TLDR:[/h2] A fun and seemingly-cozy fishing game with a dark underside.

[h2]GAMEPLAY OVERVIEW:[/h2] Dredge opens with the player arriving at the island town of Greater Marrow, learning they are replacing the previous fisherman. They are tasked by the town's mayor to get to work and catch fish to feed the town's inhabitants. Though the job seems easy, the locals warn the player to be careful outside of town, especially after nightfall.

At its core, Dredge is a cozy fishing game. There are numerous species of fish to catch, separated by geography and time of day, as some fish only come out at night. Fishing spots are marked by disturbances in the water, which can be spotted and scanned from a distance. Some fish can only be caught by certain methods (such as a rod versus a trawling net), and bottom crawling crustaceans require crab pots to nab. Each species of fish also features aberrations—monstrous deformed variants of the normal fish—that can be caught at random. Such variations are often worth more to the fish buyers, as exotic specimens, and their colorful descriptions in the player's encyclopedia set the mood for the game.

All of the player's fishing tools, lights, and engines can be upgraded with money earned from their catch. The ship's hull can also be reinforced several times, giving more room and slots for gear, and more durability, at great cost. In addition to fish, some spots offer the chance to dredge the depths, bringing up building supplies (wood, metal parts, etc.) used in upgrading, or treasures (jewelry, sextants, and others) that can be sold to certain collectors. The player may also find or be rewarded research parts used to discover more advanced equipment.

Early on, the player will meet the mysterious Collector, who sets the player on a mission to recover five lost artifacts. With each lost artifact, the player gains new abilities, such as Manifest, which brings one back to the Marrows, Haste to give you a temporary speed boost, or Atrophy, which will instantly catch all the fish in a given spot, at the risk of catching rotting or diseased fish.

The player will quickly note that something is off with the world. Aside from some of the more questionable encounters with townspeople, it becomes apparent fish aren't the only inhabitants of the oceans. Traveling at night and certain activities raise the character's panic level, which results in hallucinations, obstacles where none existed, and even attacks by submerged monsters. Collective damage to the boat will sink it and send the player back to their last save (the last time they docked). Some threats can be banished with the right skills but often, the player will have to evade or elude enemies. The varying monsters patrolling the waters have different patterns and behaviors that can be exploited.

Dredge also features a fair bit of side content. Mysterious hooded figures reside at hidden locations, demanding certain fish to sate their hunger. Fishing shrines offer riddles to be solved and pieces of a treasure map can be pulled from the depths. There are other side missions, most of them simple fetch-style quests, with tangible rewards.

Dredge's gameplay loop will probably bore some players, as it’s pretty much the same from start to finish, the new species and threats notwithstanding. For me, the real joy simply came from collecting the fish and completing the encyclopedia. The game is perfect for the OCD-types among us, seeking to catch one of everything. Aside from the general relaxation coming from catching fish (at least during the daytime), the steady pace of upgrading equipment and the ship feels like real progress.

That said, the moments of being attacked can be quite tense. Hostile mobs can be very fast and while the ship is decently maneuverable, it's still hard to evade strikes at times. Worse, colliding with anything solid (other than docks, which are visibly cushioned by old tires) damages the hull, so one can very easily sink themselves by panicking and trying to evade an attack in tight quarters. The player just has to keep their cool and, if entering an area with a known threat, go in with an escape plan ready.

[h2]STORY / WORLDBUILDING:[/h2] The story for Dredge is pretty bare-bones, at least at first glance. The behavior and dialogue of the townsfolk hint the story is more complicated and sinister than a simple job replacement. Dredge borrows heavily from Lovecraft's mythology and that influence is felt through the entire game. Successive clues and discussions as the player finds the relics build the uneasy narrative toward a grim conclusion. Depending on the player's choices, the game ends somewhere between bittersweet and disastrous.

Though Dredge takes place over the archipelago, there are hints at a wider world with civilization beyond the islands. The islands themselves are laid out well, with each cluster showcasing slightly different topography, ambience, and threats. There's enough variety in the settings to keep the game feeling fresh.

[h2]DLC:[/h2] The game has several DLC. Two—Pale Reach and Iron Rig—add new main/side quests, fish to catch, and achievements. Pale Reach concerns an icy area and a doomed expedition. Iron Rig centers around an ill-fated drilling platform. Both add a few hours of content and are worth a look. A third DLC, Blackstone Key, is really only worth purchasing to support the devs, since the items it adds don't have any lasting impact on gameplay.

[h2]TECHNICAL ASPECTS:[/h2] Dredge ran flawlessly, and I didn't have a single error or issue over 20+ hours of gameplay. The minimalist, low-polygon graphics and muted color palette work for the game, but I really have to highlight the ambient sound and music. Both are cheery and relaxing while everything in the game is calm, but grow increasingly tense and moody when the player is in tentative situations. The overall sound scheme feeds the mood perfectly.

This is a relatively easy game to max Steam achievements, though it may take a little exploration and thinking through some of the puzzles. Getting 100% also requires the Pale Reach and Iron Rig DLCs.

[h2]FINAL WORD:[/h2] Dredge is fun in a moody, chilling kind of way. I'd recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind a little "twisted" in their "cozy" gameplay.

I enjoyed this game for a little while, but now that I've reached the midgame (third of five islands), I find there isn't much to keep me interested. At its core, the gameplay boils down to catching fish so you can catch fish faster, while finding upgrades to catch other fish faster. What I hoped for from this game was a sense of uncovering the unknown, that Lovecraftian feeling of being incapable of comprehending the true shape of the world, and I just don't experience that at all in Dredge.

Here's an example: When you find your first Aberrant fish, all mutated and unearthly and so on, you bring it to the fishmonger and he says (paraphrased, of course) "Ah yeah these show up sometimes I'll give you extra money for these".

The horrors of the unknown are less 'lurking in the deep' than they are 'lurking in the fish aisle at Walmart'. All the inhabitants of the game world are already used to the horrors of the unknown, and readily acknowledge that they're there. "Ah yeah the burrowing nightmare fish took me family crest, can you go get it?" "Ah yeah I made an electrical thingy that makes the unknowable tentacled beast from the abyssal deeps go away, can you go plug it in?" There's a cult of guys that make you do fetch quests to bring them mackerel.

I can't say that the fishing gameplay makes it worthwhile, either. Whether fishing or dredging, you're going to be doing one of four fairly similar rhythm games that get old quite fast. You get a few special abilities, but they just make it a bit easier to avoid the dangers you've already learned to avoid by that point.

I will say this, though: The art is phenomenal, and the gameplay is actually quite relaxing. If you're looking for a chill game, maybe put on a podcast and fish, you might get something out of it. Otherwise, I cannot recommend Dredge at the current price point.

At last! I confess I've been anxiously awaiting the release of Dredge ever since playing the demo during Next Fest last year. And I have great news -- it does not disappoint. Dredge is an engrossing, atmospheric, mystery-bound fishing game. I actually hesitate to call it a fishing game, because there is clearly more happening beneath the water than above it, but you will spend large chunks of your time rocking on the sea, hoping to catch the big one -- or, in the case of Dredge, the weird one. When I sat down to play DREDGE, I was expecting a lax, calming game about sailing the seas and harvesting some fish. Sure, the "Lovecraftian" tag tipped me off a little, but I was sure that my innate fear of the ocean would keep me plenty entertained.

What I was NOT expecting was to walk away with DREDGE as one of my favourite games of the year in a year that has been jam-packed with amazing releases.

Seriously, this game does everything you'd want a game of this genre to do. It delivers on the fishing, it delivers on the world, the characters, the immersion and... well, that tag isn't there for no reason. In fact, it was so good that I was immediately compelled to go for 100% right after seeing the credits.

As for gameplay, it goes for a bizarre blend of a fishing minigame that you might find in a game like Stardew Valley or Animal Crossing, but it manages to sprinkle in one of the most ingenious elements from a game like Don't Starve: the Sanity (panic) meter. Trust me, you'll get used to frantically glaring at the surface of the water while that chromatic aberration kicks in.

The upgrade system helps you feel like you're truly progressing, and something that I cannot commend the game enough for is the freedom of choice. Do you want to brave the waters on the first night, slowly dredging while something larger-than-life waits beneath? Go ahead. Want to take your time, upgrading your ship as much as you can before entering a single major area? You can do that, too.

I CANNOT recommend this game enough if you're into this sort of "subtle horror" experience. If you're like me and are helplessly scared of any body of water that's more than two-feet deep, then all the better.

Definitely one of the standouts of the year, and one that I'll look back on fondly.

Perhaps not the most helpful comparison, but it put me in mind of the sailing in The Legend of Zelda: Windwaker. This vast oceans with all these little places to discover. Safe to say that this game does a lot right and a hearty recommend from me. 

The few qualms I have with Dredge are mostly centered on the lack of stuff the game can reward you with in the latter half. I had the upgrade-tree finished roughly by the midway point, and then all the materials you find and the wealth you gather are useless. Basically, the only issue I had with the game was that I wanted a reason to stay longer in the world, which could be considered just another compliment in disguise. If you enjoy exploration, collecting and the open seas, you'll enjoy this game!

Dredge is a very good, compact indie game built around a solid gameplay loop. Fishing is entertaining, quick, and convenient. Inventory management was cleverly designed and I never felt overly frustrated with it. The game encourages explorations and the quests (pursuits) progress seamlessly from point to point. Taking cues from lovecraft, over time, you will discover that there is something unsettling about the ocean. Malformed fish, frightening sea monsters, hints of the occult, and a panic meter to manage,  Dredge's biggest strength is it's atmosphere.  

Though the early nighttime sections are genuinely unsettling, once you understand the threats and learn how to avoid them, the fear drops considerably. Eventually, the supernatural creatures become more of an obstacle to manage than something you're actually afraid of. This is where I feel that they could've improved the most. 

Still, Dredge is a breakout success, and even if you do not enjoy fishing games, I believe this game is worth a playthrough. Pick this one up when you can.

Alright. **Dredge** is done and dusted....ummmm....salted....yeah, salted. Anyway, this is a pretty unique game as far as games I've played are concerned. It's a *Lovecraftian Fishing Simulator*, lol. Sound interesting? It really is.

This was fully compatible with the *Steam Deck* with zero tweaking, and it also gets about 4ish hours on a single charge.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3003243220

The core elements of **Dredge** are catching seafood via line, net, and crab pots. Most are normal, but there are also mutated versions of each. You know...horror mutations. You will also search past wrecked ships and a few sites on land. These will provide quest items, lore, and upgrade supplies/research materials.

The latter two are used to upgrade your fishing vessel as well as core ship items (your fishing items/slots, engine power, and lighting (for when you dare stay on the water overnight)). Additionally, there are towns and other docks that provide safe places to sleep, quests, and handle the actual upgrades.

All of this is paid for by selling the seafood, and later extra supplies in addition to treasures found in your travels. You will also use your cash to pay for repairs to your vessel from danage taken from creatures and from simply running into stuff, lol. Some NPCs will also give you books that, after read, offer buffs to you and your vessel. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3003243464

This all happens in the backdrop of horrible and mysterious events happening in the area and to the people. These happen at night where the greatest danger but also greatest rewards are to be had. Your ship can be attacked, can be infiltrated by mysterious creatures that corrupt your seafood hauls, and can generally create more paranoia and madness in your skipper.

So, with all this in mind, there is an overarching tale of madness with a good and a bad ending. Little by little, you start gathering the necessary items and advancing necessary quests towards the goal of solving the mystery of the game.

The graphics are very nice. Excellent use of soft tones and contrast to create an evocative world while being ever mindful of providing detail to everything. I also enjoyed the soundtrack quite a bit.

It's basically everything that i heard about it before playing. The fishing mechanics are great, and no part of the game feels particularly grindy. (well, maybe except trying to catch Open Ocean fish, only being able to find them through bait is tedious). It's a good experience that doesn't overstay its welcome, and the ending ties it together nicely. 

however, I was pretty much able to 100% the game in 15 hours of playtime. there's nothing wrong with that, but I hoped for more lore and backstory. I would have loved to collect more messages that reveal more about the world. I wish there were more conversations like the Photographer - she tells you about creatures like the turtles and crocodiles, which is even cooler because you can see them in game. And I think the ending could have had a bit more buildup story-wise. It felt a bit abrupt to see the warning about entering the final stretch of the game.

Another thing - it's not as scary as I thought it would be. There's only like 3 or 4 events that actively attack you, and they are easy to avoid once you unlock rewards from the story. The lack of variety and also the fact that you only really get attacked by 1 thing at a time means that nothing really feels that threatening after a while. The ambiance is absolutely great, though, and all the non-lethal events add a lot.

Don't get me wrong, it's a good game, I guess I'm just wishing for more content. I guess that's what DLCs are for, but you have to pay for those. Oh well.

[b]UNEXPECTEDLY one of the best surprises in my library.[/b] Honestly, I kept thinking DREDGE was “just a fishing simulator” with interesting visuals and style and left it on the backburner for way too long. But hey, it turned out nothing like I thought — behind the rod hides a full-blown adventure with a strong Lovecraftian vibe.

What really makes the game shine is its spooky atmosphere. It’s eerie at times — yet never outright scary. You don’t feel fear, you feel curiosity, and that pull to explore just a little further.

So, the fishing? Surprisingly addicting. Combined with researching the whole map and uncovering its mysteries, it keeps you hooked far longer than you expect. The real treasure here isn’t just the catch — it’s the world itself: the visuals, the music, and the mystery in every corner. DREDGE drags you in and doesn’t let go, and it’s no wonder the game has so many positive reviews.

This game started off quite strong - great atmosphere, solid but simple gameplay, good progression - But the further you got in the more anemic it started to feel. The main areas become shorter and shorter, the story doesn't really pan out, and the ambiance thins. It's not a bad game, rather that it feels like 2/5 of a great game.

I was excited to play it, and sad it left me feeling so meh about it.

I love discovering indie games like this. I’m glad I did give it a try.

The game lasts exactly as long as it needs to. I spent around 17 hours on it, even though it can be finished faster. What slowed me down (in a good way) was how strongly the opening atmosphere pulled me in—the sense of the unknown, and fear of venturing too far too soon. I spent several in-game days fishing and selling basic catches just to slowly upgrade my boat so I’d feel brave enough to leave the starting area.

Once the world opens up, the real fun begins. The map isn’t as huge as it first appears, but each island cluster brings something new—different dangers, new fish species, and fresh mechanics that are introduced naturally as the story progresses.

At first, I thought Dredge would be another one of those cozy upgrade-loop games you can play while listening to a podcast. But the music and sound design are so good that I never felt the urge to turn them off or tune out. The soundtrack is calming, the ocean sounds—wind, rain, waves—are immersive, and even the fishing and dredging sound effects are satisfying. Fish aberration design is also top-notch.

I decided not to go for 100% completion since requirements are a bit much. Instead, I focused on what felt like a natural checklist to get the most out of the story and world. I did enough side content to fill in the lore, but skipped the grind.

Highly recommended if you enjoy atmospheric exploration, a touch of horror, and smart, satisfying gameplay progression.
